Photosynthesis is the way plants turn light into usable food. A helpful analogy is a tiny solar-powered kitchen inside each leaf. Sunlight is the power source; chlorophyll, the green pigment, is like the solar panel that captures that power. The plant takes in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil, then uses the captured energy to rearrange those ingredients into sugars it can store and use. Oxygen is released as a byproduct.

That matters for people in two big ways. First, photosynthesis is the base of most food chains: the calories in wheat, rice, vegetables, fruit, and even meat usually begin as plant-made sugar. Second, it continually adds oxygen to the atmosphere and removes some carbon dioxide. So photosynthesis is not just a plant trick; it is one of the background processes that makes human life possible.
